Penn State's Agricultural Analytical Services Laboratory is on the list. It runs a mail-in kit program for homeowners and publishes its fees, which are on our cost guide.

ohio.name: Ohio
ohio.title: Ohio certified drinking-water labs: all 75 on Ohio EPA's November 2026 list
ohio.description: Every lab on Ohio EPA's November 2026 list of labs certified or accepted for drinking-water testing: 44 Ohio labs for bacteria or chemistry, plus PFAS, radiochemistry and other specialty labs, with what each category covers.
intro: Ohio EPA's Division of Drinking and Ground Waters publishes one PDF of every laboratory it has certified or accepted to test drinking water. The current edition is headed "November 2026" (the file was created October 30, 2026). We downloaded it fresh on November 11, 2026 and list all 75 labs on it below, with the categories exactly as Ohio EPA prints them.

Compared with the September 30, 2026 file this page was first built from, one lab was removed: Eurofins Environment Testing North Central (formerly Metiri Analytical Group, Inc.), 4450 Johnston Parkway, Cleveland, is no longer on the list. All other rows were checked line by line and are unchanged. The list does not say why a lab was removed.

What the categories mean: the first page of the PDF has a key. "Standard Chemistry" covers tests including nitrate, nitrite, fluoride, chloride, sulfate, hardness, pH and TDS. "Trace Metals" covers primary metals including arsenic, lead, barium and mercury, and secondary metals including iron, manganese and sodium. "Radiochemistry" includes gross alpha, gross beta, radium-226/228 and uranium. Ohio EPA adds: "Please contact individual lab(s) for detailed information about the analyses offered." A category on the list does not mean a lab runs every test in it.

For a typical private-well check (bacteria, nitrate, arsenic), look for a lab with both a bacteria entry and Standard Chemistry plus Trace Metals. Looking for PFAS? Two Ohio labs are on the list for PFAS: Alliance Technical Group in Cuyahoga Falls and Microbac Laboratories' Marietta Division. The rest of the PFAS labs are out of state (last group).

Before you call a lab, check with your local health district. Ohio EPA and the Ohio Department of Health both point private-well owners there first. See our guide to where to get well water tested in Ohio.
caveats: Ohio EPA titles this list "Laboratories Certified/Accepted to Perform Analyses on Public Drinking Water". It is a compliance list for public water systems. It does not say which labs take samples from homeowners, what they charge or how fast they report. Call first.

Ohio EPA's own disclaimer: the list "should not be construed as an endorsement", and "Other laboratories may hold acceptance for these parameters and may not appear here". Questions about a lab's status go to Ohio EPA Laboratory Certification, dwlabcert@epa.ohio.gov or (614) 644-2752.

The grouping is ours. Group 1: Ohio labs with a bacteria or chemistry entry whose names do not show a public agency. Group 2: Ohio water-utility, county and state-agency labs, which often serve only their own system. Group 3: out-of-state labs, and Ohio labs listed only for algal toxins (a surface-water test), any category.
The short descriptions on each chip (such as "includes nitrate") are abridged from the key on page 1 of the same PDF. The exact columns as printed are under each listing.
We did not verify prices, turnaround times, websites or whether any lab accepts walk-in samples, so none are shown.

new-york.name: New York
new-york.title: New York well-water labs: 23 labs named by six county health departments, plus 36 PFAS-accredited labs
new-york.description: ELAP-certified labs that New York county health departments (Westchester, Rockland, Dutchess, Saratoga, Onondaga, Tompkins) point private-well owners to, plus NYS DOH's August 2026 list of labs accredited for PFAS methods. Each listing cites its source; re-verified November 13, 2026.
intro: New York certifies environmental labs through the Department of Health's Environmental Laboratory Approval Program (ELAP) at the Wadsworth Center. Its public search tool is the authoritative way to check whether a lab is approved for drinking water (ELAP calls it potable water), and for which tests.

The search tool has no downloadable list and now runs a reCAPTCHA check, so we do not reproduce a statewide directory. Instead, this page lists the labs that six county health departments name for private-well owners: Westchester and Rockland (labs registered under each county's private-well testing law), Dutchess, Saratoga, Onondaga (which also covers Cortland and Cayuga) and Tompkins. Where the counties' lists overlap or disagree (a lab's name, ZIP code or street address), the listing says so.

Below those is a separate list from the NYS Department of Health: labs accredited in New York for the PFAS methods EPA 533 or EPA 537.1 version 2, published for its Private Well PFAS Testing and Mitigation Rebate Pilot. As of the program page revised October 2026, NYS DOH says it is accepting free PFAS testing applications from private-well households in Dutchess, Orange, Putnam, Suffolk, Ulster and Westchester counties, while funds last.
caveats: Not statewide. Only labs on the county lists below are shown in the main list. If your county is not listed, ask your county health department or use the ELAP search.

County lists differ in age: Rockland's is revised June 2026, Saratoga's June 2026, Westchester's prints no date (its file was last modified April 7, 2026), Dutchess's web page prints no date, Onondaga's page was last modified June 2025 and Tompkins's list was updated March 26, 2024.

Westchester and Rockland require a lab registered with the county for testing under their private-well testing laws (for example, at a property sale). Tell the lab why you are testing. The other counties' lists are suggestions; Saratoga says any ELAP-certified lab is fine.

We could not run the ELAP search (it needs a reCAPTCHA check), so we did not confirm each lab's current scope. We did compare lab names with the search tool's lab-name menu on November 13, 2026; each listing says whether its name appears there. Carnell Environmental Inspections (Westchester list) did not appear under that name.
We did not verify prices. None of these lists publish fees.

Tompkins County's list also includes Yaws Environmental Lab, which the county marks as not ELAP certified (a drop-off service). We left it out. Putnam County's lab list is dated February 20, 2018, so we did not use it.

maryland.name: Maryland
maryland.title: Maryland state-certified drinking-water labs for private wells (MDE list, in-state and out-of-state)
maryland.description: All 92 labs on MDE's October 1, 2026 list of certified drinking-water laboratories: 39 Maryland-based labs and 53 out-of-state labs, with approved tests in plain English and the source and verification date on every listing.
intro: The Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) says households with private wells should have their water tested periodically by a state-certified laboratory that conducts a drinking water test. MDE recommends sampling at least once a year for total coliform bacteria, nitrates, total dissolved solids and pH, and again any time the water's odor, taste or appearance changes.

MDE's Laboratory Certification Program publishes one list of every certified drinking-water lab, with its address, phone number and approved tests. Its latest revision is dated October 1, 2026; we re-checked it on November 14, 2026 and it had not changed. This page shows all 92 labs on that list: the 39 in its "In State Labs" section and, further down, the 53 in its "Out of State Labs" section. MDE's test codes ("Micro 4", "Inorganics 1" and so on) are turned into plain names using MDE's own list of approved contaminants.

We put commercial labs certified for both bacteria and at least one chemistry group first. A well owner's basic annual test needs both. Labs certified only for bacteria, or only for chemistry, are in a separate group further down.
caveats: MDE's list is the certification list for public water system compliance testing. It does not say which labs take samples from homeowners. Call the lab before you collect a sample.

Total dissolved solids and pH, two of MDE's four recommended annual tests, are not certification categories on MDE's approved-contaminant list. The list therefore can't tell you who runs them. Ask the lab.
MDE notes that evaluation of certified labs is ongoing and the list may change before its next website update. For private and real-estate testing, MDE also recommends using a certified sampler.

Out-of-state labs on MDE's list are certified by MDE, but most are large commercial labs that test for water utilities. A few are near the Pennsylvania, Virginia and Delaware lines. MDE's list doesn't say which ones take samples from homeowners, ship sample kits, or accept walk-in drop-offs.
We did not verify prices, turnaround times or websites for any Maryland lab, so none are shown.
maryland.limited_note: Each of these commercial labs is certified on MDE's list for bacteria only or for chemistry only. You may need a second lab, or the lab may send part of the work elsewhere. Ask first.

This page shows the labs located in Virginia (82 of the 147 labs on the file) and pulls out the analytes a private-well owner usually cares about: coliform bacteria and E. coli, nitrate and nitrite, arsenic, lead and copper, and so on. Labs approved for both bacteria and at least one chemistry analyte, and not run by a water utility or government agency, are listed first. That is the combination a basic well test needs.

vermont.description: The 26 labs on the Vermont Department of Health drinking-water certification list (Sept. 28, 2026) that Vermont marks as accepting private samples, with certified test groups, expiration dates and the source on every listing.
intro: The Vermont Department of Health publishes the list "Laboratories Certified for Drinking Water Analysis" (dated September 28, 2026). It has 46 certified labs, and the Department highlights in green the labs that accept private samples. This page lists those 26 green-highlighted labs, which is what a private well owner needs.

Many of the labs are outside Vermont, in New Hampshire, New York, Massachusetts and elsewhere. Free state bacteria test first: the Alabama Department of Public Health (ADPH) says about 800,000 people, or 20 percent of Alabamians, depend on private water supplies such as wells. Its collection instructions for private water samples (form CL-27, file updated September 2026) say "The fee is currently waived for each private water sample tested by the laboratory." You must use the sterilized bottles from your county health department or the lab office, fill to the 100 mL mark after running the water at least 3 minutes, and deliver the sample yourself, Monday through Thursday, 7:30 am to 4:00 pm. Samples over 30 hours old when received are not tested. ADPH's well water page says results are available about 24 hours after the sample is received, and that your county health department can send an environmentalist to collect the sample, for which "There may be a collection fee."

What the free test does not cover: the same ADPH form says the Bureau of Clinical Laboratories "does not perform any chemical analysis of private well water," and that its report "does not meet any regulatory or financial institution requirements such as mortgage". For nitrate, metals or other chemistry, use a lab on ADEM's chemical lists below; Alabama Extension (ACES) gives the same advice. If a lender or buyer needs a report, ask a certified private lab whether its report meets their requirements. ADEM says it has no authority over private wells and no funding to test them.

County fees vary. intro: Idaho does not publish a single list of certified drinking-water labs. Instead, the Idaho Bureau of Laboratories (IBL), part of the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare (IDHW), posts each lab's certificate in a public document folder linked from its Drinking Water Testing and Certification page ("View Idaho and Out of State Drinking Water Certificates for Inorganics, Organics, Microbiology, and Radiochemistry"). We opened every certificate in that folder on November 10, 2026. Together they cover 33 labs, 11 in Idaho and 22 out of state. Each listing below shows the certificates and effective dates as printed, and links the certificate itself.

IDHW says about 30% of Idaho residents use private wells as their main source of drinking water, that private wells are not regulated, and that well owners should test for bacteria and nitrate once a year and for other contaminants, including metals and chemicals, every 3 to 5 years. Its Drinking Water and Private Wells page (updated November 2, 2026) lists eight labs under "Idaho Certified Laboratories"; those eight are the first group below.

Free state testing (currently sold out): IDHW's private wells page announces "Free Idaho Private Well Water Testing (Available Fall 2026)" for nitrate, fluoride, arsenic, lead, uranium, manganese, chromium, nickel, copper, zinc, selenium, cadmium and barium. Bacteria are not on that list. Kits are requested through the Idaho Health Tools site, one kit per household every five years, and results are shared on IDHW's groundwater map without names or addresses. IDHW warns processing "may take up to two months." When we checked on November 10, 2026 the Idaho Health Tools listing was marked "Sold Out" and said testing is offered "while funding lasts."

Paying the state lab directly: IBL's Private Well Owner Drinking Water Analysis Submission Form (revised August 21, 2024, as posted in IBL's forms folder) lists these prices: total coliform/E. coli $21, nitrate $20, fluoride $20, arsenic $23, lead $23, uranium $23, copper $13, manganese $13, iron $13, hardness $28, TDS $16, and gross alpha/beta by quote. The form says bacteria samples must reach the lab within 30 hours of collection in a sterile bottle from IBL, nitrate must be tested within 48 hours, and bottles come from IBL or your local public health district. The form is more than two years old, so confirm prices with IBL at (208) 334-2235 before you send a sample.
caveats: Certification is not the same as taking homeowner samples. Certificates say what a lab is certified to test for public water systems; they do not say who accepts samples from the public, prices or turnaround. Call first and ask about bottles, fees and drop-off hours.

Chips for Idaho labs come from each certificate: an analyte is shown only if the certificate marks it "C" (certified). Chips for out-of-state labs show only which certificate types are posted, not individual tests.

Some posted certificates had already expired when we checked (for example SVL Analytical's 2025 inorganic certificate and Eurofins Edge Analytical's certificates). These are flagged on each listing. The folder may lag behind renewals, so ask the lab or IBL for current status.

The grouping is ours: the first group is the eight labs on IDHW's private wells page; the second is the other Idaho certificate holders (two city labs and a hospital lab); the third is labs outside Idaho, which hold Idaho certificates by reciprocity.
Phone numbers for the first group are from IDHW's private wells page. The certificates do not print phone numbers, so none are shown for the other labs.
We did not verify prices (except IBL's published form), turnaround times or websites for any lab, so none are shown.

montana.title: Montana certified drinking-water labs for private well testing (DPHHS list, Nov 2026)
montana.description: All 36 labs on Montana DPHHS's certified drinking-water lab list (15 in Montana), what each is certified for, which are on MSU Extension's well-owner list, and the state lab's published private-well prices.
intro: The Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services (DPHHS) runs the Water Laboratory Certification Program. Its web page lists every lab certified to analyze Montana public drinking water, in five categories: asbestos, chemistry (inorganic and organic), chemistry (inorganic only), radiologic only, and microbiology (bacteria). We transcribed that page on November 12, 2026. It lists 36 labs: 15 in Montana and 21 out of state. The page has no printed date; the server reported it was last changed on June 5, 2026.

DPHHS says certification "authorizes laboratories to analyze public water supplies in Montana." The list does not say which labs take samples from private-well owners. MSU Extension Water Quality keeps a separate list for well owners (last updated February 2023) and advises calling a lab first "to get the most up to date information on analyses, costs, and hold times." Each listing below says whether the lab is also on MSU's list.

The state lab tests private wells. The DPHHS State Environmental Laboratory in Helena says it serves "the general public" and publishes private-well forms with prices. Its chemistry form (July 2025) lists a $55 Basic Screen (coliform/E. coli, nitrate + nitrite, conductivity) and a $135 Metals Screen that includes arsenic, lead and uranium. Its bacteria form (January 2024) lists total coliform presence/absence for $25. Both forms say "prices subject to change" and require payment in advance. Call (406) 444-3444 or (800) 821-7284 to check before you send a sample.

MSU Extension's Well Educated program offers test kits through participating county offices, with guidance on what to test for in each county. MSU says the program "is not intended for real estate or legal purposes"; for those, or if you are in a hurry, it points well owners to a certified lab directly. DPHHS also runs free well-water testing for licensed or prospective childcare facilities on wells (request form linked from the State Environmental Laboratory page).
caveats: Certification is not the same as taking homeowner samples. The DPHHS list is for labs that test public water supplies. Call first and ask about bottles, fees, hold times and drop-off or shipping.

The chips show only the DPHHS category a lab is listed under. "Inorganic" covers things like nitrate and metals, but the page does not list individual tests, so ask the lab whether it is certified for the specific test you want (for example arsenic or uranium).
Bacteria samples have short hold times. The state lab's forms say bacteria samples must reach the lab within 48 hours of collection. Out-of-state labs may be hard to reach in time.

The grouping is ours: the first group is Montana commercial labs and the state lab; the second is a city utility lab, a water plant lab, a county health department lab and the Montana Bureau of Mines and Geology; the third is labs outside Montana. Labs listed in more than one category are shown once with every category.
Where the DPHHS page and MSU Extension's 2023 list print different phone numbers or addresses, the listing notes both.
Prices are shown only for the state lab, from its own published forms. We did not verify prices, turnaround times or websites for any other lab.

nebraska.title: Nebraska certified labs for well water testing (DHHS list, Nov 2026)
nebraska.description: All 5 labs on Nebraska DHHS's certified drinking-water lab list plus the state lab (NPHEL), what each is certified for, published private-well test prices, and how to order a state kit.
intro: The Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) certifies labs to test public drinking water under Title 179, Chapter 20. Its Laboratory Certification page links one "Certified Labs" PDF. We transcribed it on November 15, 2026. It lists 5 labs, all in Nebraska: three are certified only for total coliform/E. coli, one (American Agricultural Laboratory) also for nitrate/nitrite, and one (Midwest Laboratories, by reciprocity) for bacteria, nitrate, nitrite, copper, lead, VOCs and fluoride. The PDF prints no date; the file was created May 22, 2024.

The state lab is not on that PDF because DHHS runs the program. The Nebraska Public Health Environmental Laboratory (NPHEL) in Lincoln says it is certified by the U.S. EPA, and it sells kits to private well owners. The Nebraska Department of Water, Energy and Environment (DWEE) recommends testing a private well every year for bacteria and nitrate and, in a November 2024 notice, gave kit prices of $17 for bacteria and $16 for nitrate. Order kits online or call (402) 471-3935.

Private wells in Nebraska do not have to be tested by law, with some exceptions such as licensed childcare and foster homes, according to Nebraska Extension. Lenders and county health departments may require a test when a property with a well is sold. Nebraska Extension (NebGuide G1614, revised October 2022) recommends a certified lab when results may be used for a loan, legal action, or before spending a lot on treatment.

Local options: Central District Health Department in Grand Island tests private wells (coliform $27, nitrate $25 on its own page). The Southwest Nebraska Public Health Department hands out free nitrate/nitrite test strips each May and September and says to confirm any problem with a certified lab; it also says some Natural Resources Districts (NRDs) offer testing for well owners.
caveats: Certification is per test. Most labs on the DHHS list are certified only for coliform bacteria. If you need certified results for nitrate, arsenic, uranium or anything else, ask the lab before you sample.
The DHHS list is for labs that test public water systems. It does not say which labs take homeowner samples. Where a lab's own page says it does, the listing says so and links that page.
Bacteria samples are time-limited: NPHEL will not test coliform samples more than 30 hours old, and Midwest Laboratories says 24 hours. Mail early in the week.

The DHHS PDF is from 2024 and prints no revision date. American Agricultural Laboratory changed owners on September 1, 2026, after the PDF was made. DHHS's lab certification manager can confirm the current list: (402) 471-8407.

Prices come only from each lab's or agency's own page, with the date we checked. NPHEL's posted price list is headed with a 2013-2023 pricing period, so its prices may be out of date. Confirm before you send a sample.
The grouping is ours: the first group is labs with a primary source showing they serve or list homeowners (or a commercial lab), the second is a public utility lab.

louisiana.title: Louisiana certified labs for well water testing (all 49 on LDH's lists, Nov 2026)
louisiana.description: All 49 labs on the Louisiana Department of Health's certified drinking-water lab lists (bacteria and chemistry), the five LDH state labs that test private wells for $40, and what each lab is certified for.
intro: The Louisiana Department of Health (LDH) certifies labs that test drinking water under the Safe Drinking Water Act. Its Laboratory Certification page links two lists, which we transcribed on November 16, 2026: a microbiology (bacteria) list dated March 2026 with 18 labs, and a chemistry list "current as of 2/12/2026" with 32 labs. One lab (Jefferson Parish) is on both, so this page has 49 labs.

For most well owners the starting point is LDH itself. Its private well page says you can collect a bacteria sample yourself and take it to a parish health unit or LDH lab for $40 per sample, or have the parish sanitarian collect it. Orders can be placed online or in person at a parish health unit. Five LDH labs (Baton Rouge, Amite, Shreveport, Alexandria and Lake Charles) are on the bacteria list. For questions about sampling or results LDH gives 1-888-293-7020.

The only private lab on the bacteria list is Water Test, Inc. in Covington, which LDH marks "private wells only". No lab in Louisiana is on both lists except the Jefferson Parish water utility lab, so for nitrate, arsenic or other chemistry most certified options are out-of-state commercial labs (listed below) or one of three in-state commercial labs.

LDH's well-owner brochure recommends inspecting and testing a well every year for biological and chemical contaminants, and also after a hurricane, flood or major rainfall, when you notice a change in the water, or when a pregnant woman, infant, elderly person or someone with a weakened immune system lives in the home.
caveats: Certification is per test. Each card shows the well-relevant tests the lab is certified for. Chemistry labs are not certified for bacteria in Louisiana unless they are also on the bacteria list.
The lists are for labs that test public water systems. "Accepts Commercial Samples" is printed on the chemistry list, but neither list says which labs take homeowner samples. Call first.

The bacteria list is dated March 2026, and several expiration dates on it (Water Test, Inc. August 2026; City of Marksville May 2026; LDH Rapides October 2026) have passed. LDH has not posted a newer list, so ask the lab. For questions about certification, LDH gives 225-219-5200.

LDH's two pages give different sanitarian prices: the private well page says sanitarian-collected testing is $150, while the online order page (fetched the same night) lists "Sanitarian Services Well Testing" at $75 and a $150 loan letter. Confirm with your parish health unit.
Bacteria samples are time-limited. Take samples to LDH Monday-Thursday before 2:00 pm, and to Water Test, Inc. Monday-Friday before 3:00 pm.

The grouping is ours: state labs, the one private bacteria lab and in-state commercial chemistry labs first; water-utility and military labs second; out-of-state chemistry labs last, sorted by whether they are certified for nitrate and arsenic.

mississippi.title: Mississippi certified labs for well water testing (MSDH list, Nov 2026)
mississippi.description: All 5 labs on MSDH's in-state drinking-water lab list, what each is certified for, MSDH's $10 private-well bacteria sampling, and MSU Extension's free well-water screenings.
intro: The Mississippi State Department of Health (MSDH) certifies labs to test drinking water for public water systems. Its Private Well Water Testing page links one list of "private water testing laboratories participating in MSDH's Drinking Water Lab Certification Program." We transcribed it on November 17, 2026. It lists 5 labs, all in Mississippi. Two are certified for chemistry and microbiology (Micro-Methods Laboratory in Ocean Springs and NASA Environmental Services at Stennis Space Center); three for microbiology only. Only two are commercial labs. The others are a city water plant, a federal-site lab and a shipyard lab. MSDH's Environmental Laboratory Certification Program page shows the same 5 labs.

For most well owners the simplest option is MSDH itself. Apply online and an MSDH environmentalist comes to take a bacteria sample from your well. The application says you will be invoiced $10 plus a processing fee. MSDH tests private wells for bacteria only (total coliform, and E. coli if coliform is found). For nitrate, arsenic, lead or other chemicals, MSDH says to use a private lab. Call the On-Site Wastewater Call Center at 1-855-220-0192 for help applying.

Mississippi State University Extension's Mississippi Well Owner Network (MWON) holds free workshops for well owners, and well owners can have their water screened for E. coli at each program. Check the calendar on the MWON page and register ahead, or call (662) 325-1788. MWON's sample instructions say to collect the sample no more than 12 hours before dropping it off. A 2025 MSU Extension news release on a Tate County workshop also offered total coliform/E. coli screening and, for the first 21 well owners, a PFAS test. A screening is not the same as a certified lab result.

Mississippi does not require private well owners to test. MSU Extension (publication P3813, 2025) recommends testing drinking-water wells at least once a year. If E. coli is found, it says not to drink the water without boiling it first. MSDH publishes a well disinfection procedure; retest after disinfecting.
caveats: Certification is per test. MSDH's list only says "Chemistry" and/or "Microbiology". The detailed test list on Micro-Methods' card comes from the MSDH certificate the lab posts on its own site. For any other lab, ask which tests it is certified for before you sample.
MSDH's list is for labs that test public water systems. It does not say which labs take homeowner samples. Where a lab's own page says it does, the listing says so and links that page.

Out-of-state labs: MSDH does not certify labs outside Mississippi directly. It accepts other states' certification by reciprocity, but it does not publish a list of those labs, so none are shown here. To check a lab's status, MSDH's certification office is at (601) 576-7582.
Bacteria samples are time-limited: Micro-Methods says 24 hours from sampling to the lab; MSDH's Public Health Laboratory takes direct deliveries up to 28 hours after collection.

Prices come only from each lab's or agency's own page, with the date we checked. MSDH's $10 fee is from its online application and does not include the processing fee. Micro-Methods does not post prices.
The grouping is ours. The first group is MSDH's own sampling service and the commercial labs. The second is the utility, federal-site and shipyard labs on the same list.

new-mexico.title: New Mexico certified labs for well water testing (all 44 on NMED's list, Nov 2026)
new-mexico.description: All 44 labs on NMED's certified drinking-water lab list (updated 10/26/2026), what each is certified for, NMED's free nitrate, iron and fluoride screening, free arsenic screening at water fairs, and posted Santa Fe lab prices.
intro: The New Mexico Environment Department (NMED) Drinking Water Bureau certifies labs to test water for public water systems. Its Private Wells page links one list of "Certified Laboratories" and says that while NMED certifies labs for public water systems, "many of these labs also offer services to private well owners." We transcribed the list on November 18, 2026. It is dated "Last Updated: 10/26/2026" and has 44 labs: 23 in New Mexico and 21 out of state.

NMED certifies labs by groups of tests. For a well owner the key groups are M (microbiological: coliform bacteria), IO (inorganics: nitrate, fluoride and cyanide), HM (heavy metals) and RAD (radiologicals). Most New Mexico labs on the list are certified for bacteria only. Only two in-state commercial labs are also certified for nitrate (IO) and heavy metals (HM): Eurofins Environmental Testing South Central in Albuquerque and Cardinal Laboratories in Hobbs. The state lab (SLD) is too, but we found no source saying it takes homeowner samples.

NMED does not regulate private wells. Its Private Wells page recommends testing every spring for coliform bacteria and nitrate, testing for arsenic every year because it occurs naturally in New Mexico, and testing for uranium every five years. It also says to test after a new well is drilled, when buying a home with a well, after a septic failure, wildfire, flood or prolonged drought, and when someone in the home is pregnant or nursing a baby under 6 months.

NMED offers two free screenings. NMED field offices test well water free for nitrate, iron and fluoride. NMED's water fairs test arsenic, conductivity, fluoride, iron, nitrate, pH and sulfate. NMED says both are screenings, not certified lab results, and neither checks for bacteria.
caveats: Certification is by test group, and the list is for labs that test public water systems. It does not say which labs take homeowner samples. Where a lab's own site says it does, the card says so and links the site. Call the others first.

Bacteria-only labs (group M) cannot give you a certified nitrate, arsenic or uranium result. NMED's list does not break heavy metals (HM) or radiologicals (RAD) down by element, so ask whether arsenic and uranium are covered before you sample.
NMED lists city and phone only. Street addresses shown here come from the lab's own website, where it has one.
"On contract" (Y/N) on the NMED list is about whether NMED pays the lab for public water system samples. It does not affect a homeowner.

Two expiration dates are close: Red River AWWT Laboratory (11/30/2026) and NELAnalytical Laboratory (12/7/2026; NMED marks its renewal as in progress). NMED's lab-certification page also says it is not accepting new reciprocity applications for out-of-state labs until at least January 2027.
Bacteria samples are time-limited: Indepth Water Testing says 24 hours from collection to the lab, kept cold.
Prices come only from each lab's own page, with the date we checked. Only Indepth Water Testing posts prices.

The grouping is ours. The first group is NMED's free screening and the New Mexico labs whose names do not show a city, utility or state owner (we did not check who owns each one). The second is labs whose names show a city, town, water utility or the state. Out-of-state labs are last, with bacteria and nitrate labs first.

utah.title: Utah certified labs for well water testing (all 63 on DDW's list, Nov 2026)
utah.description: All 63 labs on Utah DDW's certified drinking-water lab list, which ones take outside samples, what each is certified for, and posted well-water test prices from the state lab and six county and district health department labs.
intro: Utah's Division of Drinking Water (DDW, part of Utah DEQ) links a "List of certified labs" from its Lab and sampling resources page. It is an online spreadsheet with no revision date. We downloaded it on November 19, 2026. It has 63 labs: 29 in Utah and 34 out of state. For each lab DDW shows whether it takes "Commercial Samples", whether it is PFAS-certified for drinking water, its phone and address, and a tick box for each certified analyte.

For most well owners the useful labs are the state lab and the local health department labs. The Utah Public Health Laboratory (UPHL) in Taylorsville posts its prices: $20.90 for coliform/E. coli, $17.60 for nitrate, $12.00 for pH and $14.03 for total dissolved solids, and $13.20 per metal such as arsenic or lead. Six local health department labs on DDW's list post well-water bacteria tests from $12 (Davis County) to $30 (Southwest Utah, Southeast Utah). Bear River and Southwest Utah also test nitrate ($30).

UPHL's Private Wells page says the EPA does not regulate private wells and that well owners should test at least every year for nitrate, pH, total dissolved solids and total coliform/E. coli. It also lists the tests each local health department requires or recommends for individual wells. Several (Salt Lake, Tooele, TriCounty, Utah County, Weber-Morgan) list arsenic and other metals; others require nothing. UPHL says official local health department information takes precedence over its table, so check with your county before a home sale or building permit.
DDW ticks nitrate for 13 of the 29 Utah labs, but only some of those take outside samples. Only two Utah labs are marked PFAS-certified for drinking water: UPHL and Chemtech-Ford.
caveats: DDW's list is for labs that test public water systems. "Commercial Samples?" is DDW's column; it does not define it. Several health department labs marked "NO" say on their own sites that they test private-well samples, so we list them first with their posted prices.

The analyte tick boxes are DDW's and look incomplete for some labs (for example, Chemtech-Ford is not ticked for arsenic). Treat a missing tick as "ask", not "no". Chips on each card show only well-relevant analytes that DDW ticked.
Most health department labs test bacteria only. For nitrate, arsenic or a full panel, use UPHL, a lab ticked for those tests, or ask your health department which lab it uses.

Bacteria samples are time-limited: Southwest Utah requires arrival within 24 hours; Davis County rejects coliform samples older than 30 hours, and UPHL must start testing within 30 hours. Keep samples cold, and use the lab's own sterile bottle.

Prices come only from each lab's or health department's own page or fee schedule, with the date we checked. Bear River's board approved $5 increases to two lab fees on October 19, 2026; its web page still shows the old prices.
Addresses and phones are as printed by DDW unless the card says otherwise. Where a health department's own page gives a different drop-off address or phone, the card shows both.

The grouping is ours. The first group is Utah labs that DDW marks as taking commercial samples or whose own pages say they take private-well samples. The second is the other Utah labs (city, water district, sewer district, industrial and two health department labs). Out-of-state labs are last, with bacteria and nitrate labs first.

wyoming.title: Wyoming certified labs for well water testing (all 12 on EPA Region 8's list, Nov 2026)
wyoming.description: All 12 Wyoming labs EPA Region 8 certifies for drinking water (Feb 2026 list), what each is certified for, and the published private-well prices: $8 state lab bacteria test, county and town labs, and the state agriculture lab's chemistry packages.
intro: Wyoming does not certify drinking-water labs itself. EPA Region 8 staff inspect and certify Wyoming labs for particular analytes and methods, and EPA publishes the list as a one-page PDF. We transcribed that PDF on November 20, 2026. It is headed "Current as of February 2026" and lists 12 labs, all in Wyoming. EPA notes that it also "accepts reciprocal certification for laboratories certified in other states," so out-of-state labs certified elsewhere can be used for Wyoming public water systems, but they are not on this list.

The list is written for public water systems; it does not say which labs take homeowner samples. Wyoming DEQ's Know Your Well program keeps a separate "Find a Laboratory" list "to assist homeowners," which includes some of these labs and some that are not on EPA's Wyoming list (Wyoming Analytical Laboratories in Laramie and Rock Springs, Intermountain Laboratory in Sheridan and Gillette, and labs in Billings, Montana). DEQ says to check prices with each lab and to get bottles and sampling instructions from the lab you choose.

What to test for: Wyoming DEQ recommends testing a private well "for bacteria (e. coli, total coliform) and nitrates every year," and "for arsenic, lead, copper, iron, manganese, sulfate, and total dissolved solids (TDS) every five years." It adds that uranium, radium, selenium and methane are also common in Wyoming groundwater, and that owners near oil and gas development should test for more. DEQ's well-owner helpline is 307-777-WELL (9355).

Cheapest published options we found: the Wyoming Public Health Laboratory in Cheyenne tests well water for total coliform and E. coli for $8 a sample (bacteria only). County and town labs in Jackson ($25), Rock Springs ($30 in county) and Pinedale ($35) also post bacteria-test prices. For chemistry, the Wyoming Department of Agriculture lab in Laramie posts water packages from $40 (2021 price list), and Teton Conservation District sells that lab's well kits to Teton County residents for $50 ($130 for non-residents). Only three labs on EPA's list are certified for nitrate, and one of those (Energy Laboratories, Casper) shows certification end dates that have passed.
caveats: EPA's list is dated February 2026. Certification end dates are printed per lab; Energy Laboratories in Casper shows March 31, 2026 (microbiology) and June 30, 2026 (chemistry and radionuclides), both past. EPA's page says "it is the responsibility of the water system to ensure that the laboratory certification is current for the analyte of interest." Ask the lab for its current certificate.

Chips show exactly what EPA ticked. For bacteria, "detect" means certified for presence/absence methods and "count" for counting methods. EPA has one "METALS" column and does not say which metals, so ask whether a lab is certified for arsenic, uranium or another specific metal.

No lab on EPA's Wyoming list is certified for VOCs, and only two (Energy Laboratories, Casper and Pace in Sheridan) are certified for uranium. For these tests you may need a lab certified in another state; Region 8 accepts reciprocal certification.

Bacteria samples have short hold times. The state lab requires samples within 30 hours of collection and does not accept them on Fridays; county and town labs take samples only on certain weekdays (listed under each lab).

The grouping is ours: the first group is labs with a primary source (their own page, the Wyoming Department of Health, or Wyoming DEQ's homeowner list) showing they serve the public; the second is the Cheyenne utility lab, the Lincoln Water Quality Lab in Afton, a National Park Service lab and a hospital lab, which may test only their own water.

Contact names and e-mail addresses on EPA's list are not shown. Where EPA prints a staff line and the lab publishes a main number, we show the main number and note both. Where addresses differ between EPA and the lab's own page, both are noted.
Prices come only from the labs' or agencies' own pages, with dates where printed. We did not verify prices for Energy Laboratories, Pace or the second-group labs, so none are shown.

south-dakota.title: South Dakota certified labs for well water testing (all 16 on DANR's list, Nov 2026)
south-dakota.description: All 16 labs South Dakota DANR certifies for drinking water (4 in-state, 12 out-of-state), which ones take private-well samples, and the state lab's posted per-test fees: total coliform $20, E. coli $22, nitrate $18.
intro: South Dakota certifies drinking-water labs itself, through the Department of Agriculture & Natural Resources (DANR) Drinking Water Program. DANR's Laboratory Certification page lists every certified lab: 4 in South Dakota and 12 out-of-state labs under "Other labs certified by South Dakota". We copied that page on November 21, 2026; it prints no revision date. DANR certifies labs to analyze "compliance samples from public water systems," so the list does not say which labs take homeowner samples. We checked each in-state lab's own page for that.

For a private well, the main route is the South Dakota Public Health Laboratory in Pierre (the "State Health Laboratory" on DANR's list). You order sample bottles from the Department of Health online, or pick them up at a County Extension office, and mail the sample back. In Sioux Falls, the city's Public Health Laboratory says it serves private citizens and posts well-sampling instructions (bacteria only). In Rapid City, Mid Continent Testing Laboratory has a private-well testing page.

What to test for: DANR recommends retesting a well for bacteria "at least annually," and after heavy rains, snowmelt or flooding to submit "at least a bacteriological and nitrate analysis." Nitrate above 10 mg/L (as nitrogen) matters for infants six months and younger and for pregnant women, and boiling raises nitrate rather than removing it. If a bacteria test comes back unsafe, DANR says to boil drinking water until the well tests safe.

New wells: DANR says the Centennial Environmental Protection Act of 1989 "requires that all new domestic wells drilled in South Dakota are tested for bacteria and several selected chemicals." The Department of Health's bottle order form has a "New Well" option, and Mid Continent has a New Well Sampling Program form.

Cheapest published prices we found: the state lab's fee page (updated September 22, 2026) lists total coliform at $20, E. coli at $22 and nitrate at $18 per test, plus arsenic $23, lead $18.50, uranium $26 and others (full list under the lab below). No other South Dakota lab posts prices. DANR also links a Midwest Assistance Program brochure (revised October 2023) offering free well assessments with water testing to South Dakota well owners "while funding is available"; we did not confirm the program is still funded.
caveats: DANR's page prints no revision date and no certification end dates. Ask the lab for its current South Dakota certificate if the result is for a loan, sale or permit.

Chips show DANR's broad categories as printed, not individual tests. "Inorganics" (or "IOCs") usually covers metals and minerals such as nitrate, arsenic and lead, but DANR does not itemize them, so ask whether a lab is certified for the specific test you need. "SOCs" are synthetic organic chemicals such as pesticides; "VOCs" are volatile organic compounds such as solvents and fuel components; TTHMs, HAA5s, bromate and chlorite are disinfection byproducts that matter for chlorinated public water, not usually for wells.

In South Dakota, only the state lab and Mid Continent are certified for inorganics (which typically include nitrate). The Sioux Falls city lab and American Engineering Testing are certified for bacteria only.

The grouping is ours: the first group is in-state labs with a primary source showing they take private-well or private-citizen samples; the second is an in-state lab with no such page; the third is DANR's out-of-state list.
Contact names on DANR's list are not shown. Prices come only from the labs' or agencies' own pages; we found posted prices only for the state lab.

hawaii.title: Hawaii certified labs for well and catchment water testing (all 22 on DOH's lists, Nov 2026)
hawaii.description: All 22 labs Hawaii DOH certifies or approves for drinking water: 2 in-state commercial labs for bacteria, 7 county and DOH labs, and 13 mainland labs for chemistry. Plus DOH's $25 subsidized lead and copper test for catchment homes.
intro: Hawaii's Department of Health certifies drinking-water labs through the State Laboratories Division (SLD). The Safe Drinking Water Branch's "Certified / Approved Drinking Water Labs" page now points to two SLD lists: a chemistry and radiochemistry list headed November 16, 2026 (13 labs) and a microbiology list (10 labs, file created November 18, 2026). We copied both on November 22, 2026. Eurofins in Pomona, California is on both, so there are 22 labs in all.

The short version for a private well or a rainwater catchment system: for bacteria (total coliform and E. coli), two commercial labs on Oʻahu are certified, AECOS Laboratory in Kaneohe and FQLabs in Honolulu. DOH's previous directory (November 2025) listed both as accepting private samples. For chemistry such as nitrate, arsenic or lead, every lab on the November 2026 chemistry list is on the mainland. SLD says it "approves" out-of-state labs for chemistry only and that Hawaii has no formal reciprocity agreements with other states.

Rainwater catchment: DOH says home catchment systems are not regulated, but recommends a screening test from a DOH-certified or approved lab, with the sample taken after all treatment (for example at the kitchen tap). To pass, DOH says the water should have turbidity of 5 NTU or less, no E. coli, lead of 0.010 mg/L or less and copper of 1.3 mg/L or less. DOH also subsidizes one lead and copper test per year for a legal dwelling on catchment: you pay shipping and $25.00, and DOH says AECOS is currently the only participating lab.

What to test a well for: DOH's Private Water Wells sheet (revised October 21, 2024) says there are no rules on private-well water quality in Hawaii, that the owner is responsible, and points to EPA's advice to test each year for total coliform bacteria and nitrates, plus pesticides, organic chemicals and heavy metals before first use. DOH suggests checking its Groundwater Contamination Viewer for known chemical contamination near you and comparing results with federal and state maximum contaminant levels.
caveats: DOH's lists are written for public-water-system compliance testing. DOH's own wording: "Always confirm the laboratory's current certification status with them before submitting any water samples," and use a lab that subcontracts only to other Hawaii-certified labs. Questions: Safe Drinking Water Branch, (808) 586-4258.

No in-state lab is on the November 2026 chemistry list. AECOS is DOH's approved lab for the subsidized catchment lead and copper test but appears only on the microbiology list; ask AECOS which chemistry tests it reports as certified before relying on a result for a loan or sale.

Bacteria samples have short hold times (our sampling guide lists them by lab), so the mainland labs are realistic for chemistry, not bacteria. SLD says it does not offer out-of-state approval for microbiology, yet its list shows Eurofins Pomona with certification type "Reciprocity"; we show it as printed.

Chips for mainland labs are computed from DOH's analyte matrix: a chip appears when the lab has a method printed for that analyte (for VOCs, the row "Regulated Volatile Organic Compounds"; for pesticides, any of the common pesticide rows; for PFAS, any PFAS row). Several printed expiration dates have passed but are marked "extended until renewal"; we show them as printed.

The grouping is ours. County water departments and DOH district labs are on the microbiology list but are not set up for homeowners as far as we can tell (DOH's November 2025 directory said the county labs do not accept private samples). Their addresses and phones come from that older directory or from DOH's lab pages, as cited on each card.

Prices: the only price we found from a primary source is DOH's $25 subsidized catchment lead and copper test. AECOS and FQLabs post no prices on their sites; we did not check the mainland labs' sites for prices.

massachusetts.title: Massachusetts certified labs for well water testing (all 36 on MassDEP's private-well list, checked Nov 2026)
massachusetts.description: All 36 labs on MassDEP's private-well lab spreadsheet: 22 that take residential samples, 14 that do not, each checked against MassDEP's certification database on Nov 23, 2026 for bacteria, nitrate, arsenic, PFAS and more.
intro: MassDEP does not regulate private wells in Massachusetts; your local board of health does, and it may have its own testing rules. MassDEP does not test water for individuals, but it publishes a spreadsheet of certified labs that answered its survey on whether they serve private well owners and other residential customers ("Created and published on 12/18/2025"). On it, 22 labs say they take residential samples and 14 say they do not. We copied it on November 23, 2026 and looked up every lab the same night in MassDEP's online certification database, which MassDEP says is updated daily, searching drinking-water ("Potable") certifications one test at a time. The chips on each card come from that search, not from the labs' own descriptions.

The short version: 9 of the 12 in-state labs that take residential samples are certified for drinking-water bacteria. For bacteria, nitrate, arsenic and lead under one roof, the in-state choices are Barnstable County Water Quality Laboratory (Barnstable) and Analytical Balance (Middleboro); out of state, Microbac Laboratories, Inc. (Dayville, CT), Granite State Analytical Services LLC (Derry, NH), Pace Analytical Services, LLC (Melville, NY), RI Analytical (Warwick, RI) and National Testing Laboratories, LTD (Ypsilanti, MI) also take residential samples (several by overnight mail or courier). Bacteria samples have short hold times, so a lab you can drive to usually matters for that test.

What to test: MassDEP's "Protect Your Family" guide says there is no state requirement to test a private well (a lender or local board of health may require it) but recommends testing for coliform bacteria and nitrate/nitrite initially and at least once a year, and for its "standard analysis" (arsenic, chloride, copper, fluoride, hardness, iron, lead, manganese, pH, sodium), radon, a gross alpha screen (bedrock wells only), VOCs and PFAS6 initially and at least once every ten years, or as your board of health requires. MassDEP also recommends testing before buying a home with a well, and a bacteria test after any well repair or pump or plumbing work (after disinfection and flushing).

PFAS: MassDEP's public drinking-water standard is 20 ng/L (parts per trillion) for six specific PFAS, individually or summed ("PFAS6"), and its PFAS FAQ recommends that all private wells be tested for PFAS, especially within one to two miles of a known source. Of the labs that take residential samples, 6 were certified for PFAS in drinking water on November 23, 2026: Barnstable County Water Quality Laboratory, GEL Laboratories, LLC, Granite State Analytical Services LLC, ProVerde Environmental, Inc., New England Chromachem and RI Analytical.
caveats: The spreadsheet is almost a year old. Several labs appear under different names in MassDEP's database (for example, Nashoba Analytical now appears as Eurofins Ayer, Northeast Environmental Laboratory as Eurofins Danvers, Granite State Analytical as Eurofins Derry, and Analytical Balance as Eurofins Providence (AB)). We show the spreadsheet name and note the database name on each card. Addresses and phones are the spreadsheet's; where the database prints a different phone, the card says so.

The spreadsheet's "analyses offered" column is each lab's own broad description (for example "Chemistry (PFAS, Lead, etc.)"). It is not the same as certification: some labs that list chemistry are certified in drinking water only for bacteria, or for bacteria plus pH and turbidity. Use the chips, and ask the lab to confirm it is certified for each test you order. MassDEP recommends asking the lab to put its MassDEP certification number on the report.

MassDEP's database has no radon test to search, so no lab here shows a radon chip; ask the lab whether it tests radon in water. MassDEP's lab-use guidance says there are no MassDEP certification procedures for iron and manganese in drinking water, yet the database returned "Potable" iron and manganese for some labs; we show what the database returned. The "Pesticides / herbicides" chip means at least one of atrazine, 2,4-D, simazine or alachlor.
Practical Applications (Woburn) is on the residential list, but the database showed no drinking-water certifications for it on November 23, 2026, so it is shown separately.

Prices: MassDEP says commercial labs set their own prices. We did not verify prices, turnaround times or websites for any lab, so none are shown. MassDEP's advice: get quotes from several certified labs and do not choose on price alone. Contact names and e-mail addresses printed by MassDEP are not shown.

The grouping is ours: in-state labs that take residential samples, the one with no drinking-water certification found, out-of-state labs that take residential samples, and the labs that told MassDEP they do not.

delaware.title: Delaware well water testing: free state kits and all 17 ODW-approved labs (Nov 2026)
delaware.description: Delaware DPH gives private well owners free bacteria and chemistry test kits (nitrate, fluoride, sodium, iron and more). Plus all 17 labs on the Office of Drinking Water's approved list, with which ones serve homeowners.
intro: The cheapest way to test a Delaware well is the state's own kit. The Division of Public Health (DPH) says test kits for private well owners "are available for pickup and drop-off for testing at no charge." One kit has two bottles: a bacteria bottle (total coliforms and E. coli) and a chemistry bottle (nitrate, nitrite, iron, fluoride, alkalinity, pH, chloride, sulfate, sodium and hardness). The Delaware Public Health Laboratory in Smyrna tests them.

For anything else (arsenic, lead, VOCs, pesticides, PFAS, radioactivity), you need a commercial lab. DPH says the state lab "does not test private drinking water wells for non-prescribed chemical or bacterial contaminants unless the DE Office of Drinking Water submits the sample." The Office of Drinking Water (ODW) publishes a list of 17 approved labs. We copied it on November 25, 2026; it prints no revision date, gives names only (no addresses or test lists), and says the labs are approved "to perform SDWA compliance testing" for public water systems. We checked each lab's linked website for a location and for any sign that it serves homeowners.

What and when to test: DPH says EPA and CDC both recommend annual sampling, and to test more often if someone in the home is pregnant or nursing, the water is used for infant formula, a neighbor finds a dangerous contaminant, the taste, odor, color or clarity changes, or after repairing or replacing any part of the well or plumbing. The state kit "WILL NOT be analyzed for compounds that may be in your water due to a spill or environmental release"; if you suspect that, DPH says to contact DNREC and consider bottled water for drinking and cooking.

Help with treatment: in August 2023 DPH announced a financial-assistance program for private well owners whose state-lab results show too much total coliform, E. coli, fluoride, nitrite or (for people on severely salt-restricted diets) sodium, with proof of enrollment in SNAP, WIC, SSI, LIHEAP or TANF. It covers a treatment system, installation and the first year of maintenance, and had a $200,000 budget "until funds expire or additional funding is secured." We did not confirm it is still open; DPH lists DHSS_DPH_PrivateWell@delaware.gov and 302-744-4546 option 9.
caveats: Price: DPH's current Private Drinking Water page (last updated April 2024), its Bacteriological Laboratory page and the August 2023 news release all say the kits are free. Two older DPH documents still show prices: the Environmental Laboratory page (last updated December 2023) says $2.00 each, and ODW's results brochure says $4 per kit. We go with "no charge"; confirm when you pick up.
The state kit forms say "PRIVATE HOMEOWNER USE ONLY - NOT FOR REAL ESTATE USE." For a home sale or loan, use a commercial lab.

ODW's list gives names only. Where a lab has several locations and ODW does not say which is approved (Alloway, Alpha, EMSL, Eurofins), or the link was dead, we show no street address. Addresses shown come from the page ODW links to or the lab's own contact page, not from ODW.
ODW does not list which tests each lab is approved for. Ask the lab for its Delaware approval for the exact test you need (ODW: 302-741-8630).

Several of ODW's links were broken on November 25, 2026: both Eurofins pages and the Water Testing Labs of Maryland pricing page returned 404, the ALS and EMSL links returned server errors, aerobiology.net no longer showed a lab site, and the Suburban Testing Labs link redirects to SPL. We did not link the broken ones.

The grouping is ours: the first group is the state lab plus the three listed labs whose own sites say they test well water for homeowners or real estate; the rest are on ODW's list with no homeowner page found. No prices are shown for commercial labs; we did not find any posted.
